newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Biggest Serbian opposition rally draws 400,000.
newsitem.headline: Biggest Serbian opposition rally draws 400,000.

text.p: Some 400,000 people jammed central Belgrade for an Orthodox New Year's Eve demonstration that was the biggest yet mounted against Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.

People, braving freezing cold, filled every nook and cranny of every street around Belgrade's Republic Square from late on Monday into Tuesday morning for the 57th straight day of demonstrations to force the government to reinstate November municipal election results.

There was a huge din from people blowing whistles, which has become one of the trademarks of the protest movement. Young people danced in the streets, fireworks were set off and Republic Square at one point was ablaze with flares.

The crowd, in a festive mood, was significantly bigger than the 250,000 who turned out on December 31, people who attended both events said. Cars were still streaming into the city centre at midnight.

"May both the New Years be happy for all of us and all of Serbia," said Vuk Draskovic, a leader of the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition which is demanding Milosevic reinstate the results of the annulled November 17 municipal elections in which Zajedno took 14 of Serbia's 18 biggest cities.

"We have entered both these New Years as prisoners -- there is no reason for too much elation," he said. "We must not assume the mentality of prisoners who are happy to outwit a warder in the prison yard. Serbia must free itself this year."
The protests have posed the biggest challenge to Milosevic's 10-year grip on power, but there was no apparent attempt by authorities to stop the rally and police were nowhere to be seen.

There were also large demonstrations in some of the cities where Zajedno won the annulled elections. In Nis, Serbia's second largest city, about 150,000 people heard speeches by local opposition leaders.
Big crowds were also reported in Leskovac, Smederevska Palanka and in Kragujevac, where about 50,000 people, or half the city's population, turned out.

In Belgrade some people were reportedly trampled by the crowd or pushed against walls but the extent of injuries was not immediately known. Radio stations reported dozens of people were separated from friends, spouses or children in the crowd.

A caller to independent Radio B-92 said the window of a shop in Republic Square was smashed by the crush of people but no one showed any interest in looting. The crowd was largely dispersed after 2 a.m. and streets were littered with glass from broken bottles.
Student organisers, saying the rally was not supposed to be political, at first tried to prevent Zajedno leaders from speaking but eventually let them make short speeches.
"We have begun this year with a great challenge," Zoran Djindjic, another Zajedno leader, said.
"Let this be a great victory for Serbia. Belgrade is today the centre of the world."
Organisers said they had invited Milosevic, but he did not come. Asked how he would have got on to the stage without a pass, one student said, "Well, he has a lot of authority."

Organisers said they planned a programme including choral singing, rock music and video messages from Orthodox Patriarch Pavle and British actress Vanessa Redgrave and rock singer Sting. But the chorus was drowned out by the crowd and most people could not see the video screens.
Cedomir Jovanovic, a member of the organising committee, said the students were pleased that so many people had shown up to celebrate the holiday and to support their protest.
The students are demanding educational reforms, including the sacking of the university rector.
"There is no problem with anyone addressing the crowd," Jovanovic said. "Our goal is democracy."
